So I'm very happy to say that we are at lecture number 11, and I hope I still have something new to tell you. We'll see. As usual, we start with the team. You already all know the team. And this is a program to teach people the engineering profession of building successful companies. It suddenly dawned on me that, actually, if you want to build a house, you have a process that you learn in engineering school. If you want to build a company, there is an engineering process that you have to — remember the definition of a successful company, which I keep repeating: profitable. First and foremost, profitable. Companies that are not profitable are always at a huge risk, because once the money is gone, they have to lay everybody off. And that's really sad.

Fast growing, because companies that don't grow are just not very interesting — and modest investment. What I'm teaching here is to show you, time and again, how you can use money effectively in order to build the company and not waste it. We are actually working now on building the workshops that are mentioned here every time. We will talk to you in person in the coming weeks to figure out exactly how we do the workshops so that they will be effective. And obviously there is the residency program. We work now with about four or five or six companies — I don't really remember. And it's very productive.

So what I want to talk about this time is a book called The Lean Startup. And I want to talk about what I call market beachheads. I have a hyphen here. Later on, I take the hyphen out, so you will see two H's, one after the other. So it's called "Beachhead." In Hebrew it's a rosh gesher, which means: when you try to conquer or get somewhere and there is an enemy on the other side, you put all your effort into a very small area and you penetrate with full force. The same idea applies here — if you want to build a market, you start with a very narrow market, you put all your efforts on it, you build your beachhead, you generate money, you become profitable. Now you're safe, you're not dying anymore, and you can start expanding. That's the whole idea here, which is why I call it a beachhead.

So let's look at the main points of the book, The Lean Startup. What I'm telling you now is what we're going to talk about in the lecture. We will go over it so you know what to expect, and at the end I will repeat it and we will compare the book itself to what we do here. We expand on the concept of market beachheads and growth engines — these are two different terms and I will explain the difference later on, but they are both very important in building successful companies. Then we have a guest lecturer, Oded — here he is — and he will talk about his company in the context of what I'm going to show here. We're still scratching our heads on this one. Oded and I thought it would be very interesting to present a company where we don't yet have a solution, so you can see something in the making, and maybe some of you will have great ideas for us.

I want to talk about two other examples. We'll have Oded, and then I'll bring two other examples, both of them taken from ZoomInfo, which I happen to know very well. Then we're going to talk about the notion of market-product fit and discuss two options. And at the end we'll talk about the lecture we plan for next time, which is going to be with Daniel, who sits over there. So it's going to be interesting.

For those of you — this is the book. We have a copy here. You can look at it, don't take it. And there is a Hebrew edition — that's the Hebrew edition, so you can read it in Hebrew if you want.

And honestly, I'll say it very softly so as not to disturb anyone — this should have been an article, not a book. You can get the gist of it in about 20 pages. It's very interesting, by the way, but I think what I'm going to describe takes about 20 pages. Here's what the story is. It became like the Bible in the startup community, and for a good reason — he has some really good ideas — but everybody is talking about The Lean Startup, so it's kind of the Bible. It focuses mainly on the importance of product-market fit. The whole idea is: how do you build products that the market needs, and how do you do that cost-effectively? That's the main concept of the book.

"Lean" means here that you try not to spend money before you are sure about what you're doing. So you build what's called an MVP — a minimum viable product. You do something, you get it out to the market — we'll talk about it later — you learn, and you keep improving. But the book really provides a methodology just for this process of product-market fit. It doesn't talk about the whole challenge of building a successful company.

So I think — and you may have noticed — that until today I spoke very little about the product, and for a good reason. The reason is most entrepreneurs and companies I talk to spend about 99.9%, maybe 95%, of their time thinking about the product. And they all assume: "If you build it, they will come." If I just have the right product, the whole market will discover it, the whole market will come. That's why I don't touch the notion of the product so much — because I think there's already full attention on it. What I'm looking at is all the other things that cause companies to fail.

So, taking an excerpt from the book — that's from the introduction. This is a book for entrepreneurs and the people who hold them accountable — I guess, the investors. The five principles of The Lean Startup, which inform all three parts of the book, are as follows. Entrepreneurs are everywhere. I will not delve into all of these concepts, just one of them, because we really want to hear Oded, so I don't want to spend the time now — if we have time at the end, I'll go over them.

Entrepreneurship is management — sounds very familiar to what I said. This is a profession. Validated learning: how do you do the cycle and learn? And this is the most important element. We're going to talk about build-measure-learn cycles. This is the MVP process. And innovation accounting — again, if we have time at the end, I'll go over all of these things. But number four is what the book is really focused on, and where it gives you real methodology on how to do it.

Again, this is from the book. It says: build, measure, learn. "The fundamental activity of a startup is to turn ideas into products, measure how customers" — I put an underline here, this is my highlight — "how customers respond, and then learn whether to pivot or persevere." All successful startup processes should be geared to accelerate that feedback loop.

And you can see the picture there at the end. Basically, what it says is this: minimum viable product — what do you do? You start with customer discovery. You identify a few customers and you talk to them. Let's say you've identified ten different customers. You start talking to them, they tell you what their needs are, and then you build an MVP — a minimum viable product. You heard that they want this graph, this feature, this form, whatever it is — you build it, you show it to them, and you get the feedback. They tell you, "That's great, but it should be connected here." So you do that, and basically you build the product. And all the time you ask them: "Would you buy this? Would you buy this? Would you buy this?" And when they say yes, you say, "Okay, now I have a product I can sell." That's the main thing he says — that's why I told you this could have been written in an article. That's basically what he keeps saying. You count it, you measure, you keep iterating until you get a product that people say, "Okay, that's good enough."

The reason I say he's missing some really important points is that for every product there are many potential markets or market segments. To say that you just pick a few customers — if I go back here — two things. I put a line under the word "customers." The whole question of who your customers are is far more critical than the product. I'll keep repeating it: who your customers are is far more important than the product, because they go together. And I'll talk about a few examples where if you pick this customer, you have this product — and if you pick that customer, you'll have a very different product, or a very different set of priorities or important things to do. So that's very important. The process of identifying who your customers are should precede the process of building an MVP.

When I talk about potential markets, they differ by many parameters. What features solve what problems? Let's start with that question. Different market segments have different problems that you're trying to solve — I'll bring many examples later on — and the importance of the problem being addressed. You can address a problem, you can solve a problem for the customer, but it might just not be a very high priority for that customer. You solved them a problem, but that problem isn't really what's bothering them.

I've seen many companies do that — they have a solution to a problem. But as I've learned the hard way in my first company — I think I told you this before — we had a product that dealt with an expert system for maintenance of sophisticated equipment. At the same time, there was another company selling to the same market with what was basically a CRM. And the other company was growing like crazy. We were growing, but not like crazy. So I asked the customer, "Why do you buy that product and not our product — after you told me it's a wonderful product, it's so important, it's great?" He said, "You're asking me the wrong question." I said, "What do you mean I'm asking you the wrong question?" He said, "The question you should have asked me is: if I only had a $1,000 budget — that's all I have — would I buy your product? And I would have told you: your product is third priority. I have other priorities in life." So — is the problem you're solving something the customer is actually ready to buy right now and ready to put money into? That's very important.

I'm just showing you a set of examples of how you need to think about the market: how well the product addresses the problem — is it solving it, touching it, or not doing anything? — and the language in which the problem is described or defined. I know it sounds obscure, but the same problem can be described very differently by very different customers. Same exact problem. You can see it a lot in medicine, right? You say, "I have a headache," and they have some Latin terminology for it. Same problem, two different words for it, two different ways to describe it. It happens a lot. If you are in the printing market, they call it one way. If you are in the building market, they call it a different way. Why is that important? I'll explain, and we will see it later on.

Marketing is done through language, right? You put an ad, you create a video, you put up a picture — it's all language. You try to convey an idea or a message through language. You are not sitting in front of the person giving a demo; you are doing something through language. So if you use the wrong language and the customer doesn't know what you're talking about, you've just missed it.

So it's very important to understand that for the market you go after, you use the terminology and the language they use to describe their problem. Notice how complicated this whole thing is — that most companies don't even think about it. Okay, I have this product, why is the whole world going to buy it? No. It's not price sensitivity until you get a customer saying, okay, I'm willing to pay you $5,000 for it — where is the P.O. I need to sign? Until then, you don't really have a customer. Again, my experience is that potential customers — let's call them prospects — are polite. They want to be nice to you. They don't want to tell you, nah, it's kind of okay but I'm not going to buy. They say, oh yeah, you did a nice job, this is really interesting. You know, "very interesting" in English means not interesting at all.

Okay, would you like it? Yeah, yeah, it's really nice. Nice job, really nice job. But when you say, okay, here's the P.O. for signing, they say, oh, wait a minute — now we're talking business. That's a whole different thing. So until you get customers willing to pay, you don't really know that they want it or need it. How easy or hard is it to create a list of potential prospects? Again, you might say, what does that have to do with it? Well, if you want to build the beachhead, you need to know who is on the other side. If you don't know who is on the other side, you can't really penetrate there. So even this question — we'll talk about it later — is really critical, and many, many more.

So I'm trying to show you the complexity of figuring out your beachhead, figuring out where you're going to start your sales. So let's play some market segmentation games. Okay? What is the difference between 10bis and Wolt? Well, as we all know, both of them work with restaurants and can send you food, right? Well, 10bis started with defining their customer as companies. By definition, they work with companies, and because they work with companies, they solve the lunch problem. You know, all the high-tech folks want to get lunch. So okay, we're going to provide you lunch — each one of you can order whatever you want. But they wanted to put daily limits because they don't want people to overspend. They wanted to deliver the food only to the office — if you're not in the office, you don't get it.

Things have changed since COVID, but that was the original idea. And because of that, they evolved into a company perk. So you can now use their card to buy at, you know, Chupsa. Why? Because okay, if I give you a thousand shekels a month, you can do whatever you want with it. On the other hand, Wolt was targeting the user, not the company. So they focused on what's important to the user. Arrival time — with 10bis, it arrived whenever it arrived. Where is the food? I don't know, let's call them and find out. An hour, an hour and a half. Wolt — think about it. Same service, right? Delivering food from a restaurant. But look at the different attention to different problems and you will see two different markets, completely different. Same service. Exactly the same service, two different markets.

Users pay the delivery fee and they don't complain. Why? Because they make an order and get it ten minutes later. They love it. They can talk directly to the restaurant — where is my food, you made a mistake. It's easy, right? And what happened then? Instead of evolving into a company perk like the other one, this one evolved into your general delivery service. You can do shopping with it, you can do whatever you need delivered with it. And you can see how those decisions — who is your customer and what do you focus on — will make two companies evolve in very different directions.

Okay, what are the different market segments for a VPN? Any ideas? I copied this from their site, the VPN site. So you can see — when you travel, right, and you want to watch things from your country, or the other way around while having fun, as my daughter calls it. She basically says it's a nice way of saying watching Netflix in Israel when they didn't have broadcasting rights in Israel. While on public Wi-Fi — obviously that's privacy, security, gaming — again, the same thing. So you can see that they can go after very different markets with very different messaging. Most people don't buy it for all six reasons. Most people buy it for one thing that bothers them, one thing they want to do. So you can start seeing how the market is actually very different — six very different markets, all combined into one product. It's the exact same product, but very different uses. Fitbit, Dropbox — same thing.

The people who use Fitbit can be people who exercise for fitness and want to — they're on the go all the time and they measure every step. Or the latest feature: connect to a caregiver. You're getting older and the family is worried. So it will send an alert if the pulse drops below 30 or something happens. You can see the huge spectrum of use cases that go to very different markets, very different people, very different messages. Dropbox — same thing. And I will later on, if we have time, talk about what Dropbox did with it.

So the first use case is automatic, instantaneous backup. You put a file, the moment you save it, it's saved on the cloud. You don't have to worry about it. That was before — when they came out, it was before Google Drive, Dropbox, and all of that stuff existed. One place for all your data across many devices — that's why I use it, because I have five computers and I want them to be synchronized all the time. Why do I have five computers? Don't ask. Shared files among team members, sharing very large files via links — you name it. There are probably ten different use cases, ten different markets.

So the most important thing I want you to always remember — the most difficult thing you have in front of you is finding paying customers. Not building the product, not the technology, not building the team. All of those pale compared to finding customers who are willing to pay you money. Everything else is under your control. You can hire people and fire people. You can rewrite the technology three times until it works. All of this is under your control. Customers are not under your control. They just aren't. So your focus should be on these people.

A logical approach is: first of all, you have to focus on the customer before you build an MVP. And that's the main area where I start to split from the Lean Startup concept. It talks about customers as if that's a given — kind of, you have customers. What I'm trying to tell you is, no, you don't have customers. The process of identifying who the customers are that are going to respond to you is the critical step. Once you know you're talking to a small market that behaves the same way, then it's easy to get a product to that market. But you need to get to the point where you can talk to a market.

You want to have a market segment that responds to your messaging. But how can you do it without a product? So I gave the answer before — marketing is about telling a story. That's what marketing is. If you think about it, you try to tell a story. And a story by definition is not the product — by definition, you're telling a story. So you don't need a product. You put it in text, you create a video, you create a picture. But there's no need for a real product, which means you can run a lot of tests while spending very little money. You can start — and we will talk about it later — with the simplest ones: Google Ads, LinkedIn, Facebook, emails, any other available marketing tool. It's very simple to do.

With Google Ads, you can say: anybody who searches for this phrase, I want to talk to them. With LinkedIn, you can say: anybody with that title in that area, I want to talk to them. There are ways of reaching market segments that you can think of. Okay, so you start with an idea about a market segment and you test it with copy. You have another idea for a market segment, you test it with copy. Cost? Dollars, tens of dollars, hundreds of dollars — that's about it. And you see if they respond or they don't. They don't respond — which is the case most of the time — I didn't catch the right one. And then they start to respond to a certain message. Okay, I have a market here that is responding. So what you want to focus on are two things: the messaging — what did I say that got their attention — and the responding market segment. So you start talking to them. Those who respond, you start talking to them. You might have a beachhead here. So you figure out you're talking to a market segment that might be interested in solving the problem you described or the feature you described.

I said I'd talk about Dropbox, but not at this moment. So what I want to suggest is to change the term. The term used in the Lean Startup is "product-market fit" — product is the important thing, then market. What I would say is "market-product fit" — focus on the market first, and then figure out what product fits that market segment. Actually, that's the reality.

What happens is, by first identifying your beachhead market and by talking to prospects, you solve two major challenges at once. And that's the key here — you solve two things at the same time. You discover a process and messaging that make potential prospects respond to you. Let's say you are in certain Facebook groups and people respond. Or maybe it's another social media platform where people respond to you. And you say, okay, I have this group — it's about 5,000 users — and they respond to me. I've already solved the biggest problem possible. And they respond to a certain message, which means I'm talking about something of great interest to them — which is why they respond. So you solve the marketing problem before you even start.

And second, you can develop a product or a service that fits their needs at the price they will pay. So when you start talking to them, you don't just talk about the features they want, but the value. It's very different. You say, well, that's great, I'll pay you $50 a month. Or you say, okay, I want $5,000 a year. And they say okay. I don't have to tell you that the difference between those two is whether you are alive or dead. $50 a month — chances are you're dead. So you want to make sure that what you talk about is not just the features, but whether they would pay what you think the product is worth to them. And you can do all of that at minimal cost.

Before spending any money on a team, my suggestion is always that the founder just does it, plays with it. It's easy to do. Before you hire anybody or develop a product — okay, I know what, I'll stop here and talk about this. So I would like to take the idea a little bit farther than we discussed before. Just to remind everybody: the beachhead — meaning the customers that respond to your message — is far more important than the product, because you tailor the product to them. But I'm still talking about, call it, brute force. You put some ads, you advertise, you describe what you do, and you expect people to come to you. That works. It's a really good way to start.

It's a scalable process, which means you can double the output of it with a very small increment in the input. You want something that basically works on its own. That's what you want. Like we discussed here with Oded a moment ago — he said, if I can put this engagement measurement device in, it will have a life of its own. People will start using it, it will just be useful because it gives value. It tells people what the engagement level of their presentation is.

So it will have a life of its own. That's what a growth engine is — something that has a life of its own and attracts the prospects you want to talk to. Okay, so a branding growth engine is a process, or a tool, or content. If you recall the lecture, I showed you many examples — sometimes it's a tool, sometimes it's content, sometimes it's both. But it's something that engages your prospects by doing two things. First and foremost, it gives them value. If it doesn't give value, it has a very short existence. So remember: if you really want to build a growth engine that will take your company flying, it has to be something that gives value to the users or the people who read it. And number two, it has to cost very little to you.

Otherwise it's not a growth engine. So it has something to do with a really inexpensive activity, or product, or whatever it is, that gives value. If we talk about what Odette brought up — this engagement measure — it's a tool. It will cost us a one-time effort to build it, not too much, but then it will tell people who give presentations on Zoom a useful measure. I'm talking now for half an hour — I've lost half the people. They're not sitting there anymore, their cameras are shut down, or whatever it is. I see the camera on, but they are not there. Whatever it is, it gives you value. You can see, every five or ten minutes, where the audience is — like I'm doing in here. And I see this guy working on his computer over there. He thinks I don't see him, but I do see him. But he's listening — that's really nice. And I won't say names, anyway, so you understand what I'm talking about.

Okay, so let's look at some examples just to make it more concrete. Facebook and LinkedIn — how did they grow? They had the most basic feature, which is: give us access to your address book. So you have, let's say, 200 email addresses in your address book. And then LinkedIn or Facebook sent an email to all of those people saying, "Hey, Jonathan is on Facebook — do you want to join and talk to him?" That's the way they grew. Each person was essentially an agent talking to 200 or 300 people who knew him. People would look at it because they know who I am — they're friends or not friends — and engage with it. That's the way all of these social networks grew. All of them had this feature, by the way. There were many, many social networks that died. So you have to remember that all of this is great, but you have to bring long-term value, or else you die.

Zoom Communications had two things that worked for them. Number one, it was free, it was easy to use, you didn't have to download anything. I sent you a link, you clicked on it, and you were in. And they also had good timing with COVID. They came to market at exactly the right moment with the right product, and they took advantage of it — they did a good job at that.

ZoomInfo, the one that I started, published a large directory of people in business. I've talked about it before. That was the growth engine of ZoomInfo for a long time. I'm sorry to say that in the last few years I haven't seen the engine working very well, but I'm no longer there.

Tikchak Live — I don't know if you guys remember what they do. They sell tickets. Really exciting platform, selling tickets. But what we did in order to get attention is we built a little engine that goes to every ticketing agency in Israel — there are about 25 of them — reading all the shows they sell tickets to. Ellie did it, right, Ellie? Raise your hand. And we built a product that pretty much aggregates all events, shows, and programs in Israel, presented on the web. We built a nice site — you can go look at it, Tikchak Live. And it is now having a life of its own.

Ofster — I've talked about it many times. It's the Elasticsearch tool that we designed and built, and the way we brought people to it — which is the Elastic DevOps Engineer crowd, a very niche crowd of people. But we gave them content that was tremendously useful: the meaning of the error log messages they were getting. The reason I'm talking about it is, again, because it is a growth engine — the investment is low and the growth is exponential. It brings you to profitability and fast growth. That's the whole idea here.

Remember, I said if the company doesn't grow, it's not very interesting. So you need to build an engine that will take the company forward while you are asleep or on a beach in Thailand. You want something that continues to work while you're not thinking about it. Tikchak Live works even on Shabbat, when these people keep the Shabbat — but we don't talk about it because it's not polite. And we have a hechsher from the Rabbinate. Right, exactly. And obviously it's a modest investment, because the whole definition of an engine like that is that it is low cost.

So we've talked about the relationship between a market beachhead and the jobs to be done. If you recall, the jobs to be done framework — the presentation was very interesting — it essentially talks about: what is the problem you're trying to solve?

So how do you do that? We can do it in one of two ways, and here is where it starts to get very interesting. You can sell a product, which is what most entrepreneurs think about: I have a product that can solve this problem, I'll give it to the customer, the customer will use it, and the job to be done gets done with that tool. However, there's another way of looking at it. The customer doesn't really care about the tool — he cares about the job he needs to get done. If I can do the job for him, that's wonderful. Why does he need to worry about it? If you can do the work for me and you do a good enough job and charge me fairly, then I'd rather delegate the problem to you.

Advertising agencies, right? Jobs to be done — I don't want to manage it. You're an agency, I'll give you the script, go do it. A lawyer — same thing. All I want is the agreement. I don't really care about having a lawyer in-house. I just want this agreement signed. That's it.

So the reason why a lot of companies don't look at delivering the job done is that investors look at it with the wrong eye and say, "That's not scalable, that's not interesting." I tend to differ. And here's the key issue: many products are too complex for customers to really use. We don't think about it, but many of these products are fairly complex. Take Wix, for example, which is even more interesting. The whole idea of Wix was: you can go on Wix and build your own website in half an hour or an hour. But let's look at reality. The reality is that there are a gazillion consultants who will build your site on Wix. Why? Because I don't really care about doing it myself. I'm willing to pay 100, 200, 500 shekels for somebody else to do it. I don't need to do anything. That's the reality. Customers really want the job done — they don't want to hassle with doing it themselves.

And if you build something interesting, you can really have something. Take Salesforce, for example — they have a very large market of consultants and what are called VARs, value-added resellers. These big companies actively encourage that. They have a lot of consultants, they certify them, they train them, and these people build all the applications you need.

Another interesting thing is: if you come with a tool, then you have to explain something that your prospects have never seen in their life. First of all, they don't understand what you're talking about in most cases. And second, they have doubts that it can really work. "What, this? I don't see how it works." Whereas when you say, "Let me just give you the results" — "I'll give you the legal agreement, here it is, you can read it, you don't need to see how I put it together" — "Oh, then I understand." So it's much easier to sell the job than to sell the tool to do the job. And remember, I'm talking about marketing — about explaining to people in text: here's what you're going to get. It's much easier to say "I can build you a website" than "we have a tool by which you can build a website." "What, a tool? On a computer? By myself? Forget it, I'm not doing it." You can see the difference.

The interesting thing is — and this is where it starts becoming an interesting company — if you provide the service using internal technology, like Wix does, you can start scaling it up because you reduce the internal time to develop it and you build a competitive advantage. So you can take a job that would otherwise have taken two or three days, and — you'll see this with Danielle when she talks at our next meeting — you reduce the time significantly. You can charge less than it would cost done manually, and still make a lot of money, because you can do it in a fraction of the time.

One of the companies we work with, called Beyond Data — or Bioform — that's exactly what they're developing, right, Jordan? We deliver to customers the same product they used to get, but we do it in a different way. That's the philosophy. Very common philosophy.

Another interesting element is that the market for jobs is much larger than the market for a product to do the job. Here's why: in order for a product to do the job to be economical, you have to sell it at a relatively high price, assuming the customer is going to use it all day long or frequently enough to justify the price. Whereas most customers need these jobs done on a weekly or monthly basis — not very frequently. So they can't afford the tool, and it makes no sense to them.

רק להזכיר לכם — הפגישה הבאה, ההצגה הבאה, תיעשה עם דניאל, ואני חושב שזה יהיה ממש מעניין. תנו לי להסביר למה. היא הגיעה עם חברה שהמשקיעים בעצם רצו לסגור. היא נאלצה — בעברית פשוטה, לפטר את כולם. אז היא נשארה עם מוצר, ללא עובדים, וללא כסף, והיא הגיעה אלי ואמרה, "מה אנחנו יכולים לעשות כאן?" והתחלנו לחשוב על ה-growth engines.

וה-growth engines בעצם הובילו למוצר מעט — או מאוד — שונה שמפותח בימים אלה, ויכנס לשוק בתקווה בעוד כמה שבועות. אני חושב שזה סיפור מאוד מעניין לראות מה סוג החשיבה הזה על growth engines יכול לעשות לאסטרטגיה הכוללת ולמודל העסקי שלכם. בדרך כלל, מה שקורה כשאתם מתחילים לחשוב במונחים של growth engines הוא שאתם מגיעים למודל עסקי שונה מאוד — ובהרבה מקרים הרבה יותר פשוט — מאשר קודם. אז אני מעודד אנשים לבוא בפעם הבאה. אוקיי, תודה.

In this lecture, Yonatan Stern opens by reinforcing the foundational definition of a successful company: one that is profitable, fast-growing, and built on modest investment. Against this backdrop, he introduces the central framework for the session — Eric Ries's influential book, *The Lean Startup* — while candidly noting that its core ideas could be conveyed in roughly twenty pages. The book's central contribution, he explains, is a methodology for achieving product-market fit: building products the market actually needs, validating them quickly, and doing so without wasting capital. Its key tool is the MVP, or minimum viable product — a lightweight, testable version of an idea that allows founders to learn and iterate before committing significant resources.

Stern then pivots to a concept he considers equally critical and often overlooked: the market beachhead. Borrowing from military strategy, the idea is to concentrate all energy on a narrow, conquerable market segment rather than spreading efforts thin. By dominating a small beachhead first, a company reaches profitability, stabilises itself, and only then expands. This principle of focused entry, he argues, is what separates companies that survive from those that run out of money chasing too broad a vision.

Closely related is the concept of the growth engine — a low-cost, scalable mechanism that drives customer acquisition and company growth with minimal ongoing effort. Stern illustrates this with several real examples: ZoomInfo's business directory, Tikchak Live's event aggregator, and Ofster's Elasticsearch error-log tool. In each case, the engine operated continuously, brought in users organically, and supported the path to profitability without demanding constant investment.

A particularly thought-provoking section explores the distinction between selling a product and delivering the job itself. Stern argues that customers fundamentally care about outcomes, not tools, and that many products are simply too complex for customers to adopt independently. Companies that offer the result directly — as a managed service or agency model — often find it far easier to sell, scale, and build competitive advantage. The Wix ecosystem of independent consultants and Salesforce's vast partner network serve as vivid illustrations of this dynamic in practice.

The lecture closes with a data-rich discussion of company intelligence signals drawn from Stern's ZoomInfo experience, showing how publicly available information — job titles, postings, website hooks, and financial reports — can be assembled into powerful lead-scoring and segmentation tools. A preview of the next session promises a compelling turnaround story, where growth-engine thinking transformed a near-defunct startup into a reinvented business model.

הרצאה זו של יונתן שטרן עוסקת באסטרטגיות לבניית חברות מצליחות, תוך התמקדות בשלושה מושגים מרכזיים: ראש גשר שיווקי, מנועי צמיחה ומתן ערך דרך ביצוע העבודה עבור הלקוח.

נקודת המוצא של ההרצאה היא ההגדרה של חברה מצליחה: חברה רווחית, צומחת במהירות ופועלת בהשקעה צנועה. שטרן מציג את הספר The Lean Startup כנקודת ייחוס חשובה, אך מבקר אותו על כך שהוא מתמקד בעיקר בהתאמת מוצר לשוק ומחמיץ היבטים קריטיים אחרים בבניית חברה. הספר מציג את מחזור build-measure-learn, שבמרכזו בניית מוצר מינימלי, הוצאתו לשוק, קבלת משוב מלקוחות ושיפור מתמיד — עד שהלקוחות מביעים נכונות לרכוש.

מושג ראש הגשר השיווקי מבוסס על הרעיון הצבאי: ריכוז כל המאמצים בפלח שוק צר ומוגדר, הפיכתו לרווחי, ורק לאחר מכן התרחבות. שטרן מדגיש כי יזמים נוטים לדלג על שלב זה ולנסות לכבוש שוק רחב מדי מהר מדי, מה שמוביל לכישלון.

מנוע הצמיחה הוא מנגנון שממשיך לפעול גם כשהיזם אינו עוסק בו באופן פעיל, ומביא לצמיחה אקספוננציאלית בעלות נמוכה. שטרן מביא דוגמאות מוחשיות: ZoomInfo שבנתה מדריך עסקי ציבורי שמשך תנועה אורגנית, Zoom Communications שניצלה תזמון מושלם עם מגפת הקורונה, ו-Tikchak Live שאגרגרה כרטיסים מכל סוכנויות הכרטיסים בישראל ויצרה פלטפורמה עצמאית.

דיון מעמיק נוסף עוסק בהבחנה בין מכירת כלי לבין מתן שירות. שטרן טוען שלקוחות רוצים שהעבודה תיעשה עבורם, ולא בהכרח לרכוש את הכלי שמאפשר לעשות אותה. מודל השירות קל יותר למכור, מוריד מחסומי כניסה ומאפשר להגיע לשוק רחב יותר. כשהשירות נשען על טכנולוגיה פנימית, ניתן להקטין את זמן הביצוע, לגבות פחות מעבודה ידנית ועדיין להרוויח משמעותית.

בנוסף, שטרן מציג את המושג של attributes חברתיים — תיוג חברות לפי מאפיינים כמיים כמו מספר אנשי מכירות, יחס מהנדסים לעובדים ומבנה ניהולי — ככלי לבניית רשימות prospects מדויקות וממוקדות. הוא מדגיש כי חוסר יכולת לבנות רשימה כזו מצביע על חולשה אסטרטגית יסודית.
